title: Persuade with care
subtitle: Make the case. Leave room to choose.
description: Practise emotion, evidence, social proof, and framing without crowding out judgment. Every scenario and number in this unit is fictional.

lessons.title: Stories with room to think
lessons.objective: Distinguish a relevant emotional appeal from pressure that bypasses a considered choice.
lessons.takeaway: A story can make a reason vivid; it cannot replace the evidence.
lessons.fieldwork: With a willing partner, tell a short product story and ask what claim they inferred. Correct any inference your evidence cannot support.

items.title: Feeling is information
items.teach: Emotion can help people notice what matters to them. The ethical question is how an appeal affects their understanding and freedom to decide, not whether it contains feeling.
items.say: Make a reason vivid without making refusal shameful.
items.ethics: Does this appeal illuminate their priorities or punish disagreement?
items.prompt: A buyer says wasted staff time is their main concern. Your accurate story describes one team recovering useful time, but you have no typical-results data. Which opening best supports their evaluation?
options: Lead with the story as the usual outcome.
Share the story, then ask whether that problem fits.
Avoid the story because feelings always distort judgment.
why: One experience does not establish what usually happens.
This connects a relevant example to their needs without assuming it represents everyone.
Emotion is not automatically manipulation; relevance and context matter.

items.title: An invitation or a squeeze?
items.teach: Look at what an appeal asks the listener to do with a feeling. Considering a relevant consequence differs from proving loyalty, escaping shame, or protecting a relationship by agreeing.
items.say: Examine the pressure, not just the warmth of the words.
items.ethics: Can someone decline without being made to feel disloyal?
items.prompt: Classify these fictional messages by the mechanism explicitly shown.

entries.text: Here is an accurate story about the problem you named; does it fit your team?
entries.why: The story invites evaluation against the buyer’s needs.

entries.text: After everything I have done for you, you owe me this purchase.
entries.why: Agreement is demanded as repayment for a relationship.

entries.text: Only people who do not care about their staff would decline.
entries.why: The message attacks identity rather than establishing fit.

entries.text: This option may reduce the frustration you described; shall we examine the evidence?
entries.why: The emotion leads into checking a relevant claim.

items.explain: The distinction is the stated mechanism. Tone alone does not decide whether an appeal supports choice.

items.title: When the story is too strong
items.teach: A listener may infer more from a vivid example than the speaker intended. Check that inference and supply the missing context before depending on it.
items.say: Check what your example made them believe.
items.ethics: Would you rely on a misunderstanding you helped create?
items.prompt: After your unusual success story, a buyer says, “So almost every customer gets that result.” You know the example is exceptional. To preserve informed evaluation, what comes next?
options: Ask whether they want to sign while enthusiasm is high.
Repeat that the story itself is accurate.
Clarify its exceptional nature and the available evidence.
why: Their enthusiasm rests on an inference you know is unsupported.
A technically true story does not correct the mistaken generalization.
This repairs the specific misunderstanding before the buyer relies on it.

items.title: A cause people care about
items.teach: The same distinction applies beyond selling a product. An accurate account of need can invite support without turning refusal into a judgment about the listener’s character.
items.say: Let the cause matter without making no a character test.
items.ethics: Does the invitation preserve a dignified way to decline?
items.prompt: A community organizer wants voluntary donations for a verified local need. Which message uses emotion while preserving a meaningful choice?
options: Describe the need accurately and invite questions or a decline.
Say good neighbors will donate before leaving.
Hide the emotional stakes and offer only a payment link.
why: An accurate account plus a real choice supports deliberation.
Belonging is made conditional on donating.
Removing context is not required; the audience still needs reasons to evaluate the request.

lessons.title: Proof with context
lessons.objective: Evaluate what testimonials, popularity, and endorsements can actually establish.
lessons.takeaway: Social proof tells you about other people; check whether it answers this person’s question.
lessons.fieldwork: Inspect a fictional or public testimonial and name one claim it supports and one claim it cannot establish.

items.title: Popular for whom?
items.teach: Popularity can indicate interest, but it does not by itself establish quality or fit. Ask who selected the product, what they needed, and what evidence addresses this buyer’s intended use.
items.say: Many people choosing it does not mean it fits this person.
items.ethics: Are you turning popularity into a claim it cannot support?
items.prompt: A fictional scheduling tool is popular among solo tutors. A hospital buyer asks whether it supports their complex staffing needs. What evidence should you prioritize?
options: A larger collection of tutor testimonials.
A demonstration against the hospital’s required workflows.
The total number of account registrations.
why: The users may have very different requirements.
This directly tests the claimed fit for the buyer’s intended use.
Registrations show uptake, not support for those workflows.

items.title: What each piece can show
items.teach: Different evidence answers different questions. A demonstration, an individual account, and an adoption count should not be treated as interchangeable proof.
items.say: Name the question before choosing the proof.
items.ethics: Is the evidence being asked to carry too much?
items.prompt: Match each piece of evidence to the narrow claim it can support on its own.
pairs: What the feature did in that demonstrated setup
How many accounts adopted within the stated definition
items.explain: Each has limits. None alone establishes every buyer’s future outcome.

items.title: The connection changes the weight
items.teach: An endorsement can be sincere and still have a connection that matters to its interpretation. Make a relevant incentive or relationship understandable instead of presenting the endorsement as independent.
items.say: Sincere and independent are different claims.
items.ethics: What relationship would change how the audience weighs this praise?
items.prompt: A consultant genuinely likes your product and receives a fee for each referral. You want to use their quote in a comparison guide. Which presentation gives readers useful context?
options: Label the quote as an independent expert verdict.
Remove the quote because paid people cannot have sincere views.
Disclose the referral relationship alongside the endorsement.
why: The referral incentive makes the independence claim misleading.
Payment does not prove insincerity; readers need relevant context.
Readers can consider the praise while accounting for the relationship.

items.title: The team everyone cites
items.teach: Social proof still needs context when no money changes hands. Separate who adopted an idea from evidence that it solves the new group’s problem.
items.say: Borrow the question, not somebody else’s conclusion.
items.ethics: Does another team’s success establish fit for this team?
items.prompt: A manager says, “The design team loves this meeting format, so support should adopt it.” Support handles unpredictable urgent calls. To evaluate fit, what should happen first?
options: Adopt it because internal praise is especially reliable.
Compare support’s needs with the format’s requirements.
Reject it because different teams can never share a method.
why: Enthusiasm from another setting does not settle this setting’s constraints.
This checks the relevant difference before drawing a conclusion.
A difference calls for investigation, not automatic rejection.

lessons.title: Frame without hiding
lessons.objective: Present useful comparisons while preserving information needed for a considered decision.
lessons.takeaway: A helpful frame makes tradeoffs easier to see, including the unattractive ones.
lessons.fieldwork: Show two fictional offers in a common format with total cost, scope, and one limitation each. Ask a partner which detail was easiest to miss.

items.title: Choose the comparison
items.teach: Framing directs attention to particular features of a choice. A useful frame follows the buyer’s priorities while keeping important costs and limitations available for comparison.
items.say: Focus attention without hiding the tradeoff.
items.ethics: What important downside could disappear inside this frame?
items.prompt: A fictional buyer wants predictable annual spending. Plan A costs 120 per month plus a mandatory 300 setup charge. Which presentation best serves that goal?
options: Show the first-year total of 1,740 alongside its components.
Emphasize only the 120 monthly charge.
Compare the setup fee with a daily coffee habit.
why: The total and components match the buyer’s budgeting question.
The mandatory setup cost would be easy to overlook.
The analogy distracts from the requested annual commitment.

items.title: Clarifies or obscures?
items.teach: A comparison can simplify a decision while retaining its substance. It becomes misleading when its structure hides a mandatory cost, a key limit, or the availability of refusal.
items.say: Simplify the view, not the person’s choice.
items.ethics: Can the buyer see what they must give up?
items.prompt: Classify these fictional design choices using the facts stated.

entries.text: Show both offers on the same twelve-month basis, with mandatory fees included.
entries.why: The shared basis makes the commitment comparable.

entries.text: Show one offer per week and the other per year without conversion.
entries.why: Different units make the prices unnecessarily difficult to compare.

entries.text: Put the known storage limit beside the capacity claim.
entries.why: The limitation is visible where it affects interpretation.

entries.text: Make the decline option read “I do not care about my team.”
entries.why: The wording adds shame to a legitimate refusal.

items.explain: The categories concern these stated designs, not a claim that every short summary or default is wrong.

items.title: The recommended option
items.teach: A recommendation should have an explainable basis in the buyer’s needs. An option being more profitable for the seller is not evidence that it better fits the buyer.
items.say: Recommend against a need, not against your commission.
items.ethics: Could you explain the recommendation using the buyer’s stated priorities?
items.prompt: A fictional buyer needs a basic reporting feature and has a strict budget. Both plans provide it; the premium plan adds unwanted features and pays you more. Which next move best follows their priorities?
options: Recommend premium because future needs may grow.
Recommend basic, explaining when an upgrade would become useful.
Present premium as the standard and mention basic only if challenged.
why: Unstated future needs do not override the present budget and requirement.
The recommendation fits the given facts while leaving room to revisit them.
That frame privileges your incentive and makes a suitable option harder to see.

items.title: The volunteer rota
items.teach: Useful framing applies to time and responsibility as well as prices. Compare commitments on a common basis and show consequential differences.
items.ethics: What will a person actually have to do after agreeing?
items.prompt: A volunteer compares two roles: one is advertised as “one evening” but also requires preparation; the other lists all hours. To support an informed choice, how should the organizer compare them?
options: Describe only the public-facing shift for each.
Recommend whichever title sounds more prestigious.
Compare each role’s total time commitment.
why: The preparation time affects the actual commitment.
Prestige does not answer the stated comparison problem.
A common time basis reveals the tradeoff the volunteer must evaluate.
